entry.title: Week 4 in one page: all about Tokenization

link.title: Week 4 in one page: all about Tokenization

entry.content:
About the paper

This week we dove into tokenization through a survey that works on two levels: a high-level map of the field, and a detailed reference for those who want to go deeper. Text is both the input and the output of an LLM, but before a model can process it, the text has to be split into tokens and converted into numerical values. Although this step is central, and is behind popular failures like miscounting the r’s in “strawberry”, it rarely gets the spotlight. The 32 authors aim to bring it to the surface, covering algorithms, multilingual challenges, evaluation, theory and more.

What we wrote

✍️ Writing. Rewriting the abstract skips some of the background and jumps right ahead to why we should care about the topic. Our beginner-friendly copy edits suggested some context to the Unigram algorithm in the Tokenization Algorithms section (3), explaining what it means to assign tokens probabilities, and a simplified opening of 4.1 normalization in the Pretokenization section. This is a long survey so we send you home with key points through a TL;DR: Tokenizers can be compared, updated without retraining from scratch, and if you learn only one algorithm, make it BPE.

🧠 Learning. One of the reasons tokenization matters: security. It is also the barrier between the model and natural language, leading to some of the popular failures. To work through BPE, we introduce it first intuitively, using an example. More on BPE later.

📊 Visualization. We visualize the numbers behind the significance of tokenization research: how much of a model’s parameters the vocabulary takes up Table 2.1, and in contrast how little research the topic gets Figure 2.1. Expanding on the overview figure 1.1, we emphasize the many-to-one probability mapping of token sequences to a sentence. Diving into token allocation bias between languages, a revisited figure 6.1 highlights English as the reference and compares different tokenizers. We add a comparative visualization to chapter 9, showing different approaches to grouping bytes into latent tokens.

🔬 Research. Building on the described algorithms, a follow-up on the paper proposes combining SuperBPE’s merging of words into superword tokens with SPLINTER’s morphological templates, allowing sentence-level templates to form superwords from non-adjacent words. Inspired by work on arithmetic, a second follow-up questions why models read and write with the same tokenizer, and proposes experiments that separate the two.

💻 Coding. Back to BPE: we put the code for BPE provided in the paper to the test. On the variants: PickyBPE reimplements and compares PickyBPE vs. BPE, exploring the “junk” tokens pruning threshold. BPE-Dropout explores the rate of merge skipping. Greedy vs. Shortest-Path Tokenization tackles the survey’s comparison of MaxMatch and PathPiece. While the paper gives an example of MaxMatch using more tokens, an experiment on a synthetic vocabulary shows this happens in about 25% of tested strings.

🔭 Scouting. Papers challenging the survey raise questions about the bits-per-byte metric for comparing tokenizers. After tokenization, attention and MLP layers relate tokenized fragments back to full words. Two posts look beyond fixed tokenization: one on how the optimal token size depends on the compute budget, and the other suggesting adaptive tokenization.

📣 Communication. To be updated soon
entry.summary: Our focus points from an extensive survey on tokenization

entry.title: Why Do Language Models Read and Write in the Same Tokens?

link.title: Why Do Language Models Read and Write in the Same Tokens?

entry.content:
Follow-ups worth doing

While reading the survey, I noticed that several approaches already treat input and output tokenization differently. DPE (Section 3.6) processes characters while predicting subwords. Hong et al. (2024) modify the output vocabulary and convert generated tokens back into the input representation, while Huang et al. (2025) expand the effective input vocabulary (Section 12.1).

These approaches point to a simple question: Why should the same tokenizer be optimal for both reading and writing?

The two sides have different roles. Input tokenization determines how information is represented to the model, while output tokenization also determines what the model needs to predict at each step. It affects the learning objective and the number of autoregressive steps needed to generate text. There is no obvious reason why the same tokenization should be best for both.

Still, most autoregressive language models use a shared tokenizer. This is convenient because generated tokens become part of the input in the following steps. Separating the two sides would make the architecture more complicated. But perhaps this convenience comes at a cost.

A recent paper, When Tokenization is Secretly Output Supervision (Baeumel et al., 2026), provides an interesting starting point. The authors trained small models on three-digit addition, independently varying whether the input and output were tokenized as whole numbers or individual digits. Surprisingly, output tokenization had a much stronger effect on learning and performance than input tokenization.

This raises two possible follow-ups.

1. Does it depend on what the model is trying to do?

Perhaps output tokenization dominates in arithmetic because the main challenge is computing and generating the answer. But would the same happen in tasks where understanding the internal structure of the input is more important?

One way to investigate this would be to extend the experiment to natural language tasks, such as text infilling and character-level editing. We could use a shared vocabulary that supports both character-level and subword-level segmentation, and vary the input and output tokenization independently, as in the original experiment.

Comparing performance and generalization across different tasks could reveal whether the relative importance of the two sides changes with the task.

If it does, this would suggest that using a shared tokenizer involves a trade-off between different requirements. It might also help explain why intrinsic tokenizer metrics (Section 7) do not always predict downstream performance well.

2. What if the two sides used completely different tokenization methods?

The first experiment would still use different segmentations within a shared vocabulary. But perhaps we should consider a more fundamental separation.

For example, byte-level input could allow the model to handle arbitrary text without depending on a fixed subword vocabulary, while subword-level output could reduce the number of generation steps.

This connects to the discussion of hierarchical byte-level models in Section 9, where efficient decoding remains an important challenge.

A possible experiment would compare a standard subword model, a byte-level model, and a hybrid model with byte-level input and subword-level output, under similar computational budgets.

This would require more architectural changes, and the comparison would be harder to control. Still, it could help answer a broader question: Instead of asking which tokenization method is best, should we ask which method is best for each side?

Final thought

Tokenization is usually treated as one design choice, but perhaps it is really two. Understanding the difference could change both how we design language models and how we evaluate tokenizers.
entry.summary: Input and output tokenization serve different purposes. Should we really use the same tokenizer for both?

entry.title: Seahorses and strawberries: where tokenization leaks through

link.title: Seahorses and strawberries: where tokenization leaks through

entry.content:
Why this matters

A language model is usually described as a function from text to text. The tokenizer sits in between and is meant to be invisible. Text becomes token ids on the way in, token ids become text on the way out, and the model is thought of as working on language. Two widely reported failures show that this description is incomplete. Asked how many letters r are in strawberry, models answered two. Asked whether a seahorse emoji exists, models said yes, printed 🐠 or 🐴, apologized, and tried again. The first failure happens where text enters the model and the second where text leaves it. Both happen because the model has no information about its own tokenization.

The idea

The input side: strawberry

In the Llama 3 tokenizer strawberry is one token (Section 7.1.1 of the survey). The model receives one id and one embedding. The GPT-4o tokenizer gives the same picture.

input tokens
strawberry st raw berry
` strawberry (after a space) | strawberry`  
s t r a w b e r r y one token per letter

Two of the three letters are inside the token berry. Anything it knows about the letters inside the word has to come from training data, where spellings are rarely written out, because the letters are not present in the input. The same section gives the opposite case. The string stzawbezzy is split into six fragments, so a task like “replace every r by z” requires the model to know how its tokens are built. Benchmarks such as CUTE and CharBench measure this ability, and Section 9 lists the loss of character-level information as one of the main costs of subword vocabularies. Byte-level and character-level models (Section 9.1) do not have this problem, and their sequences are several times longer. The same effect can be produced inside a subword model by writing the word with spaces, which gives one token per letter. The count is then correct.

The output side: seahorse

Unicode has no seahorse emoji. A proposal was declined in 2018.

Theia Vogel applied a logit lens to Llama 3.3 70B on the seahorse prompt. In the middle layers the residual stream decodes to sea horse, and near the end to horse together with the opening bytes of an emoji. The final projection onto the vocabulary takes the closest token. There is no seahorse token, so the closest token is some other sea or horse emoji. The model notices the mismatch only when the sampled token is fed back as input, and it then corrects itself, often into another wrong emoji.

The vocabulary determines the details of this failure. The models involved use byte-level BPE (Section 3.1). An emoji is four UTF-8 bytes, and in the GPT-4o and GPT-5 tokenizer all 64 emoji of the animal block U+1F400 to U+1F43F are the same prefix token followed by one final byte.

emoji bytes tokens
🐠 tropical fish F0 9F 90 A0 [F0 9F 90] [A0]
🐟 fish F0 9F 90 9F [F0 9F 90] [9F]
🐴 horse F0 9F 90 B4 [F0 9F 90] [B4]
🐬 dolphin F0 9F 90 AC [F0 9F 90] [AC]

The prefix token collects the probability of all 64 animals into one candidate, which means roughly “some animal emoji”. That candidate competes with text tokens such as There or Unfortunately and usually wins. After the prefix is emitted the model is committed, and the remaining choice is which byte closes the emoji. No byte value means “none”. In addition, the final byte tokens of rare emoji are among the least trained tokens in the vocabulary (Section 3.1.3).

A vocabulary with one token per emoji changes the decision itself. The probability that was collected in the prefix is now divided among 🐠, 🐴, 🐬 and the other near neighbours, and each of them receives a fraction. Under greedy or truncated decoding a text continuation such as there is no seahorse emoji can win, and no emoji is attempted. Section 2.2 of the survey discusses this difference between the probability of a string and the probability of a token sequence, and Section 14.5 on token healing describes the same prefix commitment from the prompt side. The effect depends on the decoding rule, because under sampling at temperature 1 the total probability of an emoji is unchanged, and the comparison assumes the same model with a different vocabulary. A vocabulary without emoji removes the loop, because the model outputs <unk> and cannot attempt an emoji. The belief that the emoji exists is unaffected by any of this. Asked only whether the emoji exists, GPT-5, Claude Sonnet 4.5 and Llama 3.3 70B said yes every time, in ordinary text.

Under the tokenizers in the survey

The tokenizers covered in the survey lead to different behaviour in both cases. A word-level vocabulary stores strawberry as one unit, so the letters are hidden, and it usually has no emoji, so the model writes <unk> or plain text and the seahorse loop cannot start. Standard BPE and Unigram vocabularies also hide the letters, because strawberry becomes one to three tokens. If the vocabulary is built over characters and each emoji is a single character, the emoji is one token and the probability is divided among the candidates as described above. Byte-level BPE, used by GPT-2 to GPT-5 and Llama 3, hides the letters in the same way and splits each emoji into a shared prefix and a final byte, which is the setting of the observed loop. SuperBPE and BoundlessBPE produce longer tokens that can span several words, so even more letters are hidden inside single tokens. Stochastic tokenization, such as BPE-dropout and Unigram sampling (Section 3.7), shows the model the same word in several splits during training, including splits with single letters, which gives it a way to learn what is inside its tokens. It does not change which emoji exist in the vocabulary. Pure character-level and byte-level models (Section 9.1) see every letter, so the count can be read from the input. On the output side they write an emoji byte by byte, so the model commits to the emoji block after the first byte, which is an even earlier commitment than with byte-level BPE. Latent tokenization such as BLT’s entropy patches (Section 9.2) keeps bytes at the input and output and groups them only inside the model. Letters are therefore visible, and the BLT authors report large gains on the CUTE character benchmarks over a subword model of similar size. The emoji is still produced byte by byte, so the seahorse case would behave as in a byte-level model. None of these choices removes the problem in both directions at once. Finer units help the model read letters, and coarser units for emoji help it avoid committing to an emoji it cannot complete.

What the two cases share

In both cases the model has no view of the tokenizer. On the input side it cannot look inside a token, so letters are not observable. On the output side it cannot look at its vocabulary, so it can only find out whether a token exists by emitting one and reading it back. Training does not tell the model which strings are single tokens and which are split. The tokenizer therefore does more than encode text. It sets the resolution at which the model reads, the set of things it can write in one step, and the way probability is divided among them. These choices are made before training and are not revised afterwards.

Learn more

  • Theia Vogel, Why do LLMs freak out over the seahorse emoji?, October 2025. The logit lens analysis and the byte tokens of the fish emoji.
  • Edman et al., CUTE: Measuring LLMs’ Understanding of Their Tokens, 2024. Character-level tasks including the strawberry family.
  • Land and Bartolo, Fishing for Magikarp, 2024. Detecting under-trained tokens, including unused byte tokens.
  • Survey Sections 2.2 (string and token probabilities), 3.1 and 3.1.3 (byte-level BPE, undertrained tokens), 7.1.1 (character-level benchmarks), 9 (byte-level models) and 14.5 (token healing).
entry.summary: Two well-known failures, counting the letters in strawberry and producing a seahorse emoji, show the two places where the tokenizer affects what the model can read and what it can write.

entry.title: TL;DR
entry.content:
The field is stuck

Surveys like this are long, but this one has an important goal: to move tokenization research forward.

The authors start by explaining why there is so little research on tokenization. Two reasons stand out:

  1. It’s hard to tell whether one tokenizer is better than another.
  2. Trying a new tokenizer is too expensive, because every experiment means training a full model from scratch.

The survey does offer ways around both problems, but they show up dozens of pages later. If you only read the beginning, you leave with the problems and none of the solutions.

So this post gives you 3 points you should walk away with. Two of them are those solutions, and the third is the one basic you need to know. (Maybe a few of these answers could have made it into the introduction, too.)

Point 1 · You can compare tokenizers

The standard way to score a language model is perplexity: how surprised the model is, on average, by each token. The catch is the “per token” part. Two tokenizers split the same text into different numbers of tokens, so their scores are not measuring the same thing. A tokenizer that produces more tokens spreads the same total surprisal over more of them, and looks better even though the model is not.

The fix is simple: divide the total surprisal by the number of bytes in the text instead of the number of tokens. This is called bits-per-byte. The byte count does not depend on how the text was split, so the scores become comparable.

Across languages, this still is not fair, because scripts differ in how many bytes a letter takes. For that case the survey suggests something else: take the same sentence translated into each language, and compare the total surprisal of the whole sentence, without dividing by anything.

You can even measure without training a model at all. Some metrics are computed on the tokenizer alone, such as how many tokens it produces for a given text. They take seconds to compute, so you can use them to tune the tokenizer’s settings before any training. The survey is careful here: it is still unclear how well these metrics predict model quality, and the evidence is mixed.

Point 2 · You can change the tokenizer without starting over

Trying a new tokenizer sounds like starting from zero. The model’s embedding table is tied to the vocabulary, with one row per token. Change the vocabulary and the table no longer fits, so people usually retrain the whole model.

The survey shows you don’t have to. You can take a trained model and add new tokens to its vocabulary, say for a new language or domain.

Each new token needs a vector, and that vector starts out random. To make it meaningful, you feed the model text that contains the new tokens and let it predict the next token, just like regular training. The difference is that only the new tokens’ vectors are allowed to change. The rest of the model is frozen.

You can go further and swap out the entire tokenizer. Only two parts of the model depend on the vocabulary: the embedding table at the input, and the output layer that scores every token. Both get rebuilt for the new vocabulary. Everything in between, which is where the model’s knowledge of language lives, stays frozen.

The new vectors don’t have to start out random, either. Each one can be built from the old vectors. Say the new tokenizer has a single token for tokenization, which the old one split into token and ization. The new vector starts as the average of those two. It still needs a little training afterwards, but nowhere near training from scratch.

Point 3 · BPE is the one algorithm you need to know

The third point is different. It is not a solution to a problem. It is the foundation the rest is built on.

Almost every large model today uses BPE, and the idea fits in two sentences. Start from single characters, and keep merging the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token. To tokenize new text, replay the same merges in the same order.

The survey explains BPE, but the abstract and introduction never mention it. Only much later does it say that almost every model uses it. One sentence up front would tell readers which part of the survey everything else builds on.

Bonus

Some languages pay more. The abstract and introduction say that languages with less data get split into more tokens, which makes the model more expensive to use in them. The actual number only comes much later: generating the same document with GPT-4o costs 3.8 times more in Burmese than in English. A fix shows up there too: a BPE variant that, at every step, prioritizes whichever language is currently compressed worst.

Training the tokenizer together with the model. The introduction asks whether this can be done. The answer comes much later: some models read raw bytes and learn on their own how to group them into units. The cost is speed, and that is still an open problem.

Bottom line

The opening chapters of the survey explain why tokenization research is stuck. The ways forward come much later. A one-sentence pointer to the solution next to each problem, right at the start, would give even readers who stop early something they can use.

To be fair, you can’t really TL;DR this survey. There is much more in it than these three points.
entry.summary: Three points to walk away with from the tokenization survey, and why they should come earlier in the paper.

entry.title: Papers worth knowing this week
entry.content:
1. FLEXITOKENS: Flexible Tokenization for Evolving Language Models (Owodunni et al., 2026)

This paper introduces a learnable tokenizer that operates directly on bytes and produces variable-length segments. It explores how tokenization can adapt to different inputs rather than relying on a fixed segmentation strategy.

2. Equity with Efficiency: An Empirical Study of Tokenizers for Multilingual Large Language Models (Wei et al., 2026)

This paper investigates why tokenizers often represent some languages less efficiently than others. It compares alternative tokenization strategies and explores how to improve multilingual efficiency without sacrificing downstream performance.

Together, these papers show that tokenizer design can influence both model efficiency and its ability to handle diverse languages.
entry.summary: Traditional tokenizers rely on fixed vocabularies, which can limit their ability to adapt to new domains and languages. These two papers explore alternative approaches to make tokenization more flexible and efficient.

entry.title: How BPE works but in a more intuitive way!

link.title: How BPE works but in a more intuitive way!

entry.content:
How BPE decides what a token is

Why this matters

I ran into Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) in Section 12 of this week’s paper, Tokenization: A Survey for Modern NLP.

BPE is one of the most common ways to tokenize text for language models. At first, tokenization sounds simple: split text into words and give them to the model.

But modern models usually do not work with full words. Instead, BPE learns useful subword pieces from the training data.

This matters because the choice of tokens affects how efficiently the model reads text, how it handles rare words, and sometimes even how well it learns different languages.

The idea

The basic idea of BPE is surprisingly simple:

Start with small pieces, then repeatedly merge the pair that appears most often.

Suppose our training data contains:

low
low
lower
newest
widest

At the beginning, we can imagine every word as characters:

l o w
l o w
l o w e r
n e w e s t
w i d e s t

Now we count which neighboring pairs appear often.

For example:

l + o
o + w
e + s
s + t

If l + o is the most common pair, BPE merges it:

lo w
lo w
lo w e r
n e w e s t
w i d e s t

Then it counts again.

Maybe the next frequent pair is:

lo + w

So we merge again:

low
low
low e r
n e w e s t
w i d e s t

After many rounds, the vocabulary contains a mixture of:

characters
subwords
whole words

For example:

"low"
"er"
"est"
"ing"
"un"

When we later tokenize a new word such as:

lower

the tokenizer might represent it as:

["low", "er"]

Instead of needing a separate token for every possible word.

Why not just use full words?

Imagine the model sees:

play
playing
played
player

A word-level tokenizer might need four separate vocabulary entries.

BPE can reuse pieces:

play + ing
play + ed
play + er

This means the model can handle words it has never seen exactly before.

For example:

unhelpfulness

could be split into something like:

["un", "help", "ful", "ness"]

The exact split depends on the tokenizer and its training data.

The important consequence

BPE learns its vocabulary from frequency, not from linguistic rules.

It does not know that -ing is a grammatical suffix.

It only learns that some character sequences often appear together.

This means common words may become one token:

"computer"

while rare words may require several:

"electroencephalography"
→ ["elect", "ro", "ence", ...]

So BPE is basically a compression-like algorithm that discovers useful repeated pieces of text.

The interesting part is that these pieces become the basic units the language model learns from.
entry.summary: How BPE decides what a token is.

entry.title: A clearer Figure 6.1: corpus share and token counts relative to English

link.title: A clearer Figure 6.1: corpus share and token counts relative to English

entry.content:
The original

Figure 6.1 on page 43 of Tokenization: A Survey for Modern NLP compares each language’s share of BLOOM training text with its total token count. The negative relationship is visible, but comparing specific languages and understanding the size of the gaps takes more effort.

I first reproduced the graph using all 1,012 FLORES-200 devtest sentences per language, for the same 41 languages. The Spearman correlation rounds to the paper’s -0.899.

The redesign

I use one row per language, ordered by its BLOOM corpus share, from largest to smallest. The percentage appears beside the language name. The horizontal axis shows how many tokens are needed relative to English, using a separate English baseline for each tokenizer.

I chose this graph because I wanted to see the differences between languages more directly. Sorting by BLOOM corpus share lets us follow the languages from more to less training text, while the percentages keep the actual shares visible. English gives a simple reference: 2× means twice as many tokens for the translated content. The three colored points in each row also make it easier to compare the tokenizers without switching between graphs.

For example, Byte-level BPE (BLOOM) needs about 2.45× as many tokens for Kikuyu as for English. For Malayalam, the ratios are about 1.38× for Byte-level BPE (BLOOM), 2.62× for WordPiece (mBERT), and 1.38× for Unigram (XLM-R).

What changed and why

  • Sort by BLOOM corpus share: follow the languages from more to less training text.
  • Print the percentages: see the corpus shares beside the language names.
  • Use English as the reference: read the relative token-count gaps directly.
  • Highlight English and the 1× line: make the reference easy to find.
  • Add two other tokenizers: compare their language gaps in the same row.

There is a trade-off: equal spacing between rows shows the order, but not the size of the differences in corpus share. The percentages and ordering describe BLOOM only; they are not training shares for mBERT or XLM-R.

Each tokenizer has its own English baseline. The graph compares relative gaps between languages, not model quality. A low token count can also be misleading if text becomes unknown tokens, so the notebook checks this separately. The relationship with corpus share alone does not prove causation.

Code

Download the notebook

The notebook includes the code and saved results. It downloads the public inputs when first run.

Sources: Tokenization: A Survey for Modern NLP, Figure 6.1, page 43; BLOOM, Table 1; FLORES-200.

entry.title: Rewriting the abstract of Tokenization - A Survey for Modern NLP

link.title: Rewriting the abstract of Tokenization - A Survey for Modern NLP

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The abstract is very long, which is adequate for such a comprehensive survey, though I thought it can be more concise, and highlight the extra contributions the survey has other than systemization of knowledge. Also, the abstract spends many words on sub words vs. character, and it feels that those are considerations anyone slightly familiar with the concept of tokenization will know.

Before and after

Before While modern language models take raw text as their input and produce raw text as output, they do not operate over text directly. Hidden in the very first step of language model pipelines is tokenization, where raw text is converted to a sequence of tokens which the model is designed to process. The dominant approach to tokenization is subword tokenization, which uses tokens whose granularity lies between that of characters (or bytes) and words. Subword tokenization is ubiquitous in modern natural language processing (NLP) due to its advantages: compared to word-level models, it solves the out-of-vocabulary problem while constraining the vocab ulary size, reducing the number of embedding parameters and logits needed. Compared to character-level models, it improves the inductive bias of models by packing more information into a token while producing significantly shorter sequences. While this technique is powerful, it is not without flaws. To name a few: it imposes a rigid system for how tokens are built, and one system may not generalize across languages; segmentation ambiguities create room for adversarial attacks; in multilingual settings, bal ancing the token allocation between high- and low-resource languages must be done explic itly; and the reliance on a static, pre-computed vocabulary means the tokenization process is disjoint from the model’s training, preventing true end-to-end optimization. There is substantial room for innovation in this domain, yet progress is contingent upon a clear un derstanding of existing methodologies and current bottlenecks. This survey aims to serve that purpose. We present tokenization in the context of the modern large language model (LLM) era and cover the breadth of areas that tokenization directly influences. We discuss algorithms, techniques, pitfalls, theory, and practice, along with jumping-off points for prospective re searchers and practitioners. We hope that this survey brings more attention to the field of tokenization as an area in which much progress is still to be made.
After Language models never see text. They see the output of a tokenizer: a pipeline of normalization, pretokenization, a vocabulary, and a segmentation algorithm that together decide what a model can represent. These choices underlie some of the most visible LLM failures, including brittle arithmetic and spelling, adversarial vulnerabilities, and a “token tax” that makes the same content cost more in many languages. Yet tokenization made up a small fraction of 2025 NLP and ML papers. We argue this neglect of tokenizers' research is structural: tokenizer ablations are costly and noisy at scale, perplexity is not comparable across tokenizers, and benchmarks typically freeze the tokenizer. This neglect is also visible through the confomism regarding choice of tokenizers - we complement the survey with a census of over 420k Hugging Face models and an audit of frontier tokenizers, open and closed. Together they reveal a monoculture: BPE with 100–275k vocabularies, and 94% of models reusing another model’s tokenizer exactly. We survey the field across the whole pipeline and model lifecycle: subword algorithms and pretokenization, writing systems and multilinguality, evaluation, non-canonical tokenizations, byte-level, latent and pixel-based alternatives, changing the tokenizer of a trained model, security, and theory. We hope that this survey brings more attention to the field of tokenization as an area in which much progress is still to be made. Each section closes with open questions, and we identify evaluation as the main bottleneck to progress.

The general rule

I wanted the abstract to actually hold the contribution, and aim for someone that is somewhat familiar with the topic, not to start “from scratch” - it’s redundant and doesn’t allow to say what’s importnat to the actual readers.

What I’m unsure about

  1. Maybe the new abstract is too concentrated on the “other than SoK” parts, and misses the SoK centrality of this paper.
  2. Maybe I’m “jumping” ahead too much and the original abstract is better for “beginner readers”?
  3. The strctural claim appears in the papaer but i gave it a more central posistion and maybe I’m incorrect in understanding the papaer (hard to get a full grasp on such a msiive paper).
entry.summary: A more concise and contribution centered rewrite of the abstract.

entry.title: Beyond Fixed Tokenization: New Strategies
entry.content:
This week’s survey discusses several limitations of traditional subword tokenization, including its reliance on fixed vocabularies and segmentation rules that cannot adapt during model training, as well as challenges in generalizing across languages. It also explores alternative approaches, such as byte-level modeling, and highlights the trade-off between sequence length, model performance, and computational cost - emphasizing that fewer tokens do not necessarily mean faster or better models.

The following two papers build on these ideas: the first addresses the computational limitations of byte-level generation, while the second further investigates how tokenization choices affect model efficiency.

1. Fast Byte Latent Transformer (Kallini et al., 2026)

This paper makes byte-level language models faster at generating text by allowing them to predict multiple bytes at once, rather than generating them one by one. The survey discusses Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) as an alternative to traditional subword tokenization, but highlights the computational challenges of byte-level generation. This paper builds on BLT and proposes techniques to make generation more efficient.

2. Compute Optimal Tokenization (Limisiewicz et al., 2026)

This paper investigates how the amount of text represented by each token affects language model efficiency, showing that the optimal degree of token compression (token size) depends on the available computational budget. The survey emphasizes that shorter token sequences do not necessarily mean faster or better models. This paper investigates that trade-off and shows why choosing the right tokenization strategy matters for efficient model training.
entry.summary: Two papers extending the survey's discussion: one addressing the noted limitations of byte-level generation, and the other further exploring the claim of why fewer tokens don't necessarily mean greater efficiency.

entry.title: copyedit 4.1
entry.content:
What I changed and why

I chose to rewrite the beginning of section 4.1, due to it being overly formal and complex.

Before and after

Before One common preprocessing step is to normalize the input text into a standardized form before tokenization. This may involve removing unwanted artifacts, mapping equivalent surface forms to a common representation, or applying lossy simplifications intended to reduce superficial variation in the data. Common surface-level transformations include: ... (good examples) These normalizations are often used to unify minor typographical differences across scripts for easier processing or to clean up erroneous text. Invisible character removal is also important for tokenizer safety, as control characters can be used to inject token breakpoints to alter a model’s output while leaving the surface form of the text unchanged (see also Section 14.3; Boucher et al., 2022).
After Before tokenization, text is often normalised into a standard format, Such that artifacts, escape or control characters do not exist. This is to prevent mapping of two visually similar text to different tokens and consequently different embeddings. ... (examples) Further more, control characters can be used to inject token breakpoints to alter a model’s output. Removing such "invisible characters" helps circumvent that safety risk.

The general rule

Use simple words to convey a simple idea.
entry.summary: One sentence that makes people want to click.
